title: The Difference Between Confidence and Evidence
summary: Feeling sure is only reliable under certain conditions. When to trust a gut call, what to ask before you commit, how much evidence is enough and how to bound a claim.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

faqs.q: When can you trust an expert's intuition?
faqs.a: When the environment is regular enough to learn and the person has practiced with accurate, timely feedback on their decisions. Those are the conditions Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein agreed on in their 2009 paper. Without them, feeling certain says little about being right.

faqs.q: How much evidence do you need before making a decision?
faqs.a: Enough to act, scaled to how hard the decision is to undo. Jeff Bezos suggested most decisions can be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had, especially reversible ones. Changes that are hard to reverse, like data migrations, deserve more.

faqs.q: How do you disagree with a confident colleague without making it personal?
faqs.a: Point at evidence you can both look at: logs, test results, user sessions. Asking "what would change your mind?" turns the disagreement into a plan for what to check next.

html:
"I'm pretty sure this will work." In a planning meeting, that sentence moves things along. It's short, it sounds decisive and it makes approval easy. Evidence rarely sounds that tidy. It shows up as a flaky test run, a support ticket, a rollout that stalled at 10%, a dashboard that got slower last week, or a teammate saying the plan doesn't match what they see in the code. Confidence and evidence often travel together, but they're different things, and teams get into trouble when they treat one as the other.

When feeling sure means something

Sometimes feeling sure is earned. Daniel Kahneman spent his career documenting how intuition goes wrong. Gary Klein spent his studying firefighters and nurses whose intuition was remarkably good. In 2009 they wrote a paper together to map where each view holds, and ended up agreeing on the conditions. In Klein's words, intuitive expertise needs "a regular situation as opposed to a chaotic and hypercomplex situation," plus "the opportunity for practice accompanied by accurate and timely feedback on the consequences of decisions" (Klein, Conversations with Kahneman). The paper's abstract (American Psychologist, 2009) ends with a line worth keeping close: "Subjective experience is not a reliable indicator of judgment accuracy."

Software has both kinds of environment. A senior engineer who has chased this service's memory leaks a dozen times, and found out within minutes whether each guess was right, has earned a fast gut call. The same engineer estimating a six-month migration, or predicting how users will react to a redesign, is somewhere else entirely: the feedback is slow, sparse and tangled up with other changes. The feeling of certainty is identical in both cases. Only one of them has been trained.

So a good first question about any confident claim is: has this person, or this team, had fast and honest feedback on this kind of call before? If yes, lean on the instinct and verify cheaply. If not, the confidence is mostly familiarity in a nicer jacket.

Ask what would change your mind

One habit helps more than any other. Before you commit to a view, ask "what evidence would make me change my mind?" If the honest answer is "nothing," the decision has probably become part of someone's identity, and arguing harder won't help. If the answer is specific, you now have a plan: run the benchmark, watch three user sessions, rebuild the incident timeline, build a throwaway prototype, try a small rollout.

The question also takes the heat out of disagreement. In a room that rewards confidence, the most polished speaker can become the source of truth by accident. When asking for evidence is normal, a teammate who rarely speaks first can say "I get the argument, but the logs show a different pattern," which is far easier to work with than "I don't trust your gut." People end up arguing about the logs instead of about each other.

How much evidence is enough

There's a trap on the other side. Some people dodge decisions by asking for one more data point, forever. It looks like rigor and works like delay. Jeff Bezos put a number on it in his 2016 shareholder letter: "most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had." Waiting for 90%, he wrote, usually means you're being slow, and "being slow is going to be expensive for sure" (2016 Letter to Shareholders).

That advice leans on another idea from the same letter: many decisions are reversible, "two-way doors" that can use a light process. How much evidence you need depends on how hard the decision is to undo. A feature flag you can flip back tomorrow needs a smoke test and a dashboard. A migration that rewrites customer data needs a lot more. If you want to dig into that half, there's a whole post on reversible decisions.

Say what you're sure of, and where it stops

In practice, the confident statements worth trusting come with a boundary:

  • "I'm confident this helps the first customer segment. I don't have evidence for the enterprise case yet."
  • "The query is fast enough at today's volume. We need a guardrail before launch, because I haven't tested it at ten times the load."
  • "I believe in this direction, and if activation stays below last quarter's number for two weeks, we revisit it."

Each one keeps the conviction and names the edge. The team learns what's known, what isn't and which signal would change the plan. That's much easier to build on than a flat "trust me," and it leaves you an honest way to be wrong later without losing face.

The goal is confidence that answers to something. Teams that pair the two can move fast and still change course when reality disagrees, and that holds up far better over time than certainty does.

Try this week

  • Next time you say "I'm pretty sure," add one sentence on what would change your mind.
  • Before you trust a gut call, ask whether the person has had fast feedback on this kind of decision.
  • For one open decision, write down how reversible it is and size the evidence to match.
  • Rewrite one confident claim in your team's current plan as a bounded one.
